'''John Broward''' "'''Brad'''" '''Culpepper''' (born May 8, 1969) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1992 to 2000. Culpepper was as an [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] when he played [[college football]] for the [[Florida Gators football|Florida Gators]]. Selected late in the tenth round of the [[1992 NFL draft]], he became a consistent starter for the [[Minnesota Vikings]], [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]], and [[Chicago Bears]].

Culpepper is also known for appearing on two seasons of the American reality television show ''[[Survivor (American TV series)|Survivor]]'', appearing on ''[[Survivor: Blood vs. Water]]'' (with his wife, Monica, of ''[[Survivor: One World]]'') and ''[[Survivor: Game Changers]]''.

== Early life ==

Culpepper was born in [[Tallahassee, Florida]] in 1969.<ref name="pfrprofile">{{Cite web |title=Brad Culpepper Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/C/CulpBr20.htm |access-date=2024-10-08 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>  He attended [[Leon High School]] in Tallahassee,<ref>databaseFootball.com, Players, {{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20100920101217/http://databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=CULPEBRA01 Brad Culpepper]}}.  Retrieved June 2, 2010.</ref> where he was a standout prep player for the Leon Lions [[high school football]] team.{{citation needed|date=August 2017}}

Culpepper was born into a family of [[University of Florida]] alumni.<ref name=hairston>Jack Hairston, ''Tales from the Gator Swamp'', Sports Publishing, LLC, Champaign, Illinois, pp. 29–31 (2002).</ref>  His father, Bruce Culpepper, was a center for the [[Florida Gators football|Gators football]] team from 1960 to 1962 and co-captain of their 1962 [[Gator Bowl]] team, and became a prominent Tallahassee attorney.<ref name=hairston/>  His uncle, Blair Culpepper, was a Gators fullback in 1957 and 1958, and became a bank president in [[Winter Park, Florida]].<ref name=hairston/>  His grandfather, [[J. Broward Culpepper]], was also a Florida graduate and served as the chancellor of the [[State University System of Florida]].<ref>University of Florida, George A. Smathers Libraries, [http://web.uflib.ufl.edu/spec/pkyonge/Culpepper.htm Guide to the J. Broward Culpepper Papers].  Retrieved April 27, 2011.</ref>

== College career ==

Culpepper accepted an athletic scholarship to attend the University of Florida in Gainesville, Florida, where he played for coach [[Galen Hall]] and coach [[Steve Spurrier]]'s Gators teams from [[1988 Florida Gators football team|1988]] to [[1991 Florida Gators football team|1991]].<ref name=ufmediaguide>''[http://web.gatorzone.com/football/media/2011/media_guide.pdf 2011 Florida Gators Football Media Guide] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120402035222/http://web.gatorzone.com/football/media/2011/media_guide.pdf |date=April 2, 2012 }}'', University Athletic Association, Gainesville, Florida, pp. 88, 93, 97, 98, 100, 124, 153, 180 (2011).  Retrieved August 28, 2011.</ref>  During his senior season in 1991, Culpepper was a standout [[defensive tackle]] and team captain on the Gators' [[Southeastern Conference]] (SEC) championship team, a first-team All-SEC selection and a consensus first-team All-American.<ref name=ufmediaguide/><ref>''2012 NCAA Football Records Book'', [http://fs.ncaa.org/Docs/stats/football_records/2012/Awards.pdf Award Winners], National Collegiate Athletic Association, Indianapolis, Indiana, pp. 9 & 14 (2012).  Retrieved September 14, 2012.</ref>  He finished his college career with eighteen [[quarterback sack]]s and 47.5 [[tackle (football move)|tackle]]s for a loss.<ref name=ufmediaguide/>  He was also named to the SEC Academic Honor Roll all four years, was a first-team [[Academic All-America]]n, and received the [[William V. Campbell Trophy|Draddy Trophy]] recognizing him as college football's most outstanding student-athlete.<ref name=ufmediaguide/><ref>"[https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=_EBWAAAAIBAJ&sjid=UOoDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6565,3758625&dq=associated+press+all-america+team&hl=en Another day, another honor for Culpepper]," ''The Gainesville Sun'', p. 7C (December 12, 1991).  Retrieved January 17, 2013.</ref>  While Culpepper was a Florida undergraduate, he was also an active member of [[Sigma Chi]] [[Fraternities and sororities|fraternity]] ([[List of Sigma Chi chapters|Gamma Theta]] chapter).{{citation needed|date=August 2017}}

Culpepper graduated from Florida with his bachelor's degree in history after his junior year, and enrolled in a master's degree program in exercise and sports sciences during his senior football season. He was inducted into the [[List of University of Florida Athletic Hall of Fame members|University of Florida Athletic Hall of Fame]] as a "Gator Great" in 2001.<ref>F Club, Hall of Fame, [http://www.gatorfclub.org/hall-of-fame/greats Gator Greats].  Retrieved December 13, 2014.</ref><ref>"[http://www.gatorzone.com/story.php?id=2815 Nine Former Gators Enshrined into the Hall of Fame] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121004070654/http://www.gatorzone.com/story.php?id=2815 |date=2012-10-04 }}," GatorZone.com (April 6, 2001).  Retrieved July 21, 2011.</ref>  The sports editors of ''[[The Gainesville Sun]]'' ranked him as the No. 47 all-time greatest player of the first 100 seasons of the Florida Gators football team in 2006.<ref>Robbie Andreu & Pat Dooley, "[http://www.gainesville.com/article/20060718/GATORS70/60718042 No. 47 Brad Culpepper]," ''The Gainesville Sun'' (July 18, 2006).  Retrieved April 4, 2013.</ref>

== Professional career ==

Culpepper was a tenth round selection (264th overall pick) in the [[1992 NFL draft]] by the Minnesota Vikings,<ref>{{Cite web |title=1992 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1992/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-07 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> and he played for the Vikings from {{NFL Year|1992}} to {{NFL Year|1993}},<ref>Minnesota Vikings, History, [http://www.vikings.com/team/history/alumni.htmler=  Alumni]{{dead link|date=November 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}.  Retrieved May 13, 2010.</ref> the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] from {{NFL Year|1994}} to {{NFL Year|1999}},<ref>Tampa Bay Buccaneers, History, [http://www.buccaneers.com/team-and-stats/history/all-time-roster.html All-Time Roster] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090916002113/http://www.buccaneers.com/history/coachesroster.aspx |date=September 16, 2009 }}.  Retrieved May 13, 2010.</ref> and the [[Chicago Bears]] in {{NFL Year|2000}}.<ref>Chicago Bears, History, [http://assets.chicagobears.com/assets/tradition/AllTimeJerseyNumbers2006.pdf All-Time Jersey Numbers] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100331052354/http://assets.chicagobears.com/assets/tradition/AllTimeJerseyNumbers2006.pdf |date=March 31, 2010 }}.  Retrieved May 13, 2010.</ref>  In his nine-year professional career, Culpepper played in 131 games, started 83 of them,<ref name=pfrprofile/> and recorded 34 [[quarterback sack]]s and one [[Safety (American football score)|safety]].<ref name=nflprofile>National Football League, Historical Players, [http://www.nfl.com/players/bradculpepper/profile?id=CUL595056 Brad Culpepper].  Retrieved May 13, 2010.</ref>

== Life after football ==

After finishing his professional playing career, Culpepper returned to graduate school and law school full-time, and earned his master's degree and [[Juris Doctor|J.D.]] degree from Florida in 2001.

Culpepper is now a trial lawyer for the Culpepper Kurland law firm in [[Tampa, Florida]].<ref>Culpepper Kurland, PLLC, Attorneys, [http://www.ckfirm.com/Bio/BradCulpepper.asp Brad Culpepper] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090531115918/http://www.ckfirm.com/Bio/BradCulpepper.asp |date=May 31, 2009 }}.  Retrieved May 13, 2010.</ref>  Since his retirement, he has spoken out about his concerns regarding the increasing size of NFL players; he believes that the increasing number of {{convert|300|lb|kg|adj=on}} players is "unnatural and unsafe" and has led to many serious health problems. During his football career, Culpepper inflated his weight to {{convert|280|lb|kg}}; after he retired from professional football, he lost almost {{convert|100|lb|kg}}.<ref>Mike Bianchi, "[http://www2.ljworld.com/news/2003/aug/05/tell_it_like/  Tell it like it is: These guys are too fat]," ''Orlando Sentinel'' (August 5, 2003).  Retrieved May 13, 2010.</ref>

===''Survivor''===

====''Blood vs. Water''====
Prior to his appearances, Culpepper's wife Monica was selected as a participant for ''[[Survivor: One World]]'', the twenty-fourth season of the CBS reality television show ''Survivor''.<ref name=deggans1192012/>

Monica and Brad participated together in the series's twenty-seventh season, ''[[Survivor: Blood vs. Water]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.realityblurred.com/realitytv/archives/survivor_blood_vs_water/2013_May_13_cast|title=Survivor Blood vs. Water cast includes Big Brother winner, former NFL player|author=Andy Dehnart|author-link=Andy Dehnart|publisher=Realityblurred.com|date= May 13, 2013|access-date=September 24, 2014}}</ref> Culpepper was the sixth person eliminated from the game and came in fifteenth place, while Monica was the season's runner-up.<ref name="l289">{{Cite web |last=Spata |first=Christopher |date=2017-02-08 |title=Tampa's Brad Culpepper returning to 'Survivor' for reality series' 34th season |url=https://www.tampabay.com/tampas-brad-culpepper-returning-to-survivor-for-reality-series-34th-season/2312525/ |access-date=2024-10-08 |website=Tampa Bay Times}}</ref>

On May 6, 2015, it was revealed that Culpepper was one of sixteenth former male players eligible to be voted onto ''Survivor''<nowiki>'</nowiki>s 31st season, ''[[Survivor: Cambodia]]''. However, he was not voted onto it.<ref>[http://www.ew.com/article/2015/05/20/survivor-cambodia-second-chance-cast-revealed Survivor: Cambodia—Second Chance cast (and logo) revealed] Entertainment Weekly, Retrieved May 21, 2015</ref>

====''Game Changers''====

On February 8, 2017, Culpepper was revealed to be one of the contestants competing in ''[[Survivor: Game Changers]]'', the show's 34th season, which began airing in March 2017. Throughout Culpepper's second season, he played relatively consistently, and stayed loyal to his alliances, despite being in the minority for the most part. However, at his endgame, he won five individual immunity challenges; a feat shared only by a few other elite Survivor players, which propelled him to the Final Three with [[Sarah Lacina]] and "Troyzan" Robertson. Although Culpepper played a solid social game and was a prominent threat, he became very arrogant and made some remarks toward fellow tribe mate Tai Trang that other players perceived as condescending in the last few days. Fellow tribemate Aubry Bracco in her jury speaks video controversially said she had hesitations about voting for Brad to win because of his "racist and sexist tendencies". At the Final Tribal Council, Lacina's skillful strategic and social gameplay was preferred by the jury over Culpepper's physical dominance, and she was awarded the title of "Sole Survivor" in a 7–3–0 vote. Culpepper received three votes, making him the runner-up.<ref name="e757">{{cite magazine | last=Chavez | first=Chris | title=Brad Culpepper finishes second on Survivor: Game Changers | magazine=Sports Illustrated | date=2017-05-25 | url=https://www.si.com/nfl/2017/05/25/brad-culpepper-runner-up-survivor-game-changers-season-finale | access-date=2024-10-08}}</ref>

his lost in the gulf tale |publisher= Tampa Bay Times |last= Shelton |first= Gary |date= March 7, 2009 |access-date= September 22, 2014 |archive-url= '''Sterling Bradford Shearer''' (born August 10, 1955) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive lineman]] for three seasons with the [[Chicago Bears]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL).  He played [[college football]] for the [[Texas Longhorns football|Texas Longhorns]], earning [[unanimous All-American]] honors and recognition as the best college interior lineman in the country in 1977.  A third-round pick in the [[1978 NFL draft]], he played professionally for the NFL's [[Chicago Bears]].

== Early life ==

Shearer was born in [[Houston, Texas]].<ref name=nflprofile>National Football League, Historical Players, [http://www.nfl.com/player/bradshearer/2525428/profile  Brad Shearer].  Retrieved June 26, 2012.</ref>  He graduated from [[Westlake High School (Texas)|Westlake High School]] in [[Westlake Hills, Texas]],<ref name=dbfprofile>databaseFootball.com, Players, {{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20120601104309/http://databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=SHEARBRA01  Brad Shearer]}}.  Retrieved June 26, 2012.</ref> a suburb of [[Austin, Texas|Austin]], where he played for the Westlake Chaparrals high school football team.

== College career ==

Shearer received an athletic scholarship to attend the [[University of Texas at Austin]], where he played for the [[Texas Longhorns football]] team from 1974 to 1977.<ref name=utprofile>TexasSports.com, Football, All-Time Lettermen, [http://www.texassports.com/genrel/shearer_brad00.html  Brad Shearer Profile].  Retrieved June 26, 2012.</ref>  He was a two-time All-[[Southwestern Conference]] selection in (1975, 1977),<ref>TexasSports.com, Football, [http://www.texassports.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/fb-all-conference.html  All-Conference] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110919144314/http://www.texassports.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/fb-all-conference.html |date=September 19, 2011 }}.  Retrieved June 26, 2012.</ref>  As a senior team captain in [[1977 Texas Longhorns football team|1977]], he averaged ten tackles per game, led the Longhorns to a No. 1 ranking,<ref name=utprofile/> and was recognized as a consensus first-team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]].<ref>''2011 NCAA Football Records Book'', [http://fs.ncaa.org/Docs/stats/football_records/2011/Awards.pdf  Award Winners], National Collegiate Athletic Association, Indianapolis, Indiana, p. 7 (2011).  Retrieved June 26, 2012.</ref>  He was also awarded the [[Outland Trophy]], recognizing him as the best interior lineman during the 1977 college football season.<ref name=utprofile/><ref>Associated Press, "{{usurped|1=[https://archive.today/20130124162032/http://news.google.com/newspapers?id=WoJJAAAAIBAJ&sjid=wwsNAAAAIBAJ&pg=4110,2414602&dq=brad-shearer+outland+trophy&hl=en  Shearer Named Outland Winner]}}," ''The News and Courier'' (December 11, 1977).  Retrieved June 26, 2012.</ref>

== Professional career ==

The Chicago Bears picked Shearer in the third round (74th pick overall) of the [[1978 NFL draft]],<ref>Pro Football Hall of Fame, Draft History, [http://www.profootballhof.com/history/story.aspx?story_id=2012  1978 National Football League Draft] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110610041930/http://www.profootballhof.com/history/story.aspx?story_id=2012 |date=2011-06-10 }}.  Retrieved June 26, 2012.</ref> and he played for the Bears from {{NFL Year|1978}} to {{NFL Year|1981}}.<ref name=nflprofile/>  In three NFL seasons, he appeared in thirty-four regular season games for the Bears, and started two of them.<ref name="pfrprofile">{{Cite web |title=Brad Shearer Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/S/SheaBr20.htm |access-date=2024-05-23 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>  He did not play during the {{NFL Year|1979}} regular season,<ref name=pfrprofile/> and his pro career was later cut short by a knee injury.<ref>Associated Press, "[https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=6b4yAAAAIBAJ&sjid=Ye8FAAAAIBAJ&pg=5545,573042&dq=brad-shearer+knee+injury&hl=en  Bears pay Shearer for wounded knee]," ''Ottawa Citizen'' (December 11, 1986).  Retrieved June 26, 2012.</ref>

'''Bradley Jay Butler, Jr.''' (born September 18, 1983) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Guard (American football)|guard]] and [[Offensive tackle|tackle]] for the [[Buffalo Bills]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the Bills in the fifth round of the [[2006 NFL draft]]. He played [[high school football]] at [[E.C. Glass High School]] and [[college football]] for the [[Virginia Cavaliers football|Virginia Cavaliers]].

==College career==
Butler is one of three Cavaliers in school history to start four consecutive bowl games. He started 31 consecutive games at right tackle, the longest streak at the [[University of Virginia]] since 1998.  As a senior, Butler started all 11 games he played.  Butler drew attention in 2005 when he hit Boston College defensive end [[Mathias Kiwanuka]] with a chop-block in the back of his knees several seconds after the whistle, in what is referred to as "the cheap shot heard 'round the ACC."<ref>Archived at [https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211210/LZpxj30vZwo Ghostarchive]{{cbignore}} and the [https://web.archive.org/web/20201119194339/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LZpxj30vZwo Wayback Machine]{{cbignore}}: {{cite AV media| url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LZpxj30vZwo| title = Cheap shot on Mathias Kiwanuka, UVA@BC 2005 | website=[[YouTube]]}}{{cbignore}}</ref>  
Butler was suspended for the following game by his own team as a result of the dirty late hit. He won the Rock Weir Most Improved Player Award in 2005.

'''Brad Elliott Scioli''' (born September 6, 1976) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[defensive end]] for the [[Indianapolis Colts]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL).

==College career==
Scioli attended [[Penn State University]], playing defensive end for coach [[Joe Paterno]]. Following a senior campaign in 1998, during which he recorded ten [[Quarterback sack|sacks]], he was named the outstanding senior member of the Penn State team.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.personal.psu.edu/dept/psusportsinfo/football/1998/120798scioli.html|title=Football Honors and Awards}}</ref> Scioli was also named defensive player of the game at the 1999 [[Hula Bowl]] college all-star game.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.personal.psu.edu/dept/psusportsinfo/football/1998/012599scioli.html|title=Football Honors and Awards}}</ref> Scioli spent a season playing [[tight end]] while in college.

Scioli earned a bachelor's degree in Hotel, Restaurant and Institutional Management from Penn State.

==Professional career==
Scioli was selected as the 138th overall pick by the Indianapolis Colts in the fifth round of the [[1999 NFL draft]] and played for the team from 1999 to 2006.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1999 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1999/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He recorded 15 [[Quarterback sack|sacks]] in his six-year career, with a high of seven sacks in 2002. He was drafted with a fifth-round [[NFL Draft|draft]] selection acquired from [[St. Louis Rams|St. Louis]] for the Colts' star running back [[Marshall Faulk]] (also included in the deal was a second-round pick used on LB [[Mike Peterson]]). Scioli retired in 2004 due to injuries.

==Personal life==
After retiring from football with a shoulder injury, Scioli went back to school at West Chester University, where he earned his certification to teach. He then got a master's degree in education development & strategies at Wilkes University. Scioli then moved back to his home town of [[Bridgeport, Pennsylvania]], which is in the [[Upper Merion Area School District]]. Following his move, in 2007 he began teaching health and physical education at Upper Merion Area High School. Scioli is married and has two daughters.{{citation needed|date=January 2025}}

==Lawsuit against the NFL==
In December 2011, Scioli was part of a group of 11 other professional players who filed a lawsuit against the [[National Football League|NFL]]. The players and their attorneys alleged that the League failed to properly treat head injuries in spite of prevailing medical evidence and the prevalent use of [[Toradol]] administered by the team to the players as a pain-masking agent, leading the players to develop effects of brain injury.<ref name=seegerweiss>{{cite web | url=http://www.seegerweiss.com/news/Seeger_Weiss_Represents_Former_NFL_Players_in_Concussion_Lawsuit | title=Seeger Weiss Represents Former NFL Players in Concussion Lawsuit | publisher=Seeger Weiss LLP | accessdate=2012-03-25 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120313043144/http://www.seegerweiss.com/news/Seeger_Weiss_Represents_Former_NFL_Players_in_Concussion_Lawsuit | archive-date=2012-03-13 | url-status=dead }}</ref>

'''Brad M. Edelman''' (born September 3, 1960) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Guard (American football)|guard]] for the [[New Orleans Saints]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). Edelman played [[college football]] for the [[Missouri Tigers football|Missouri Tigers]].

==Biography==
Edelman was born in [[Jacksonville, Florida]], and is Jewish.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QNaczbX4f78C&q=%22Brad+Edelman%22+%22jewish%22&pg=PA160 |title=The 100 Greatest Jews in Sports: Ranked According to Achievement |author= B. P. Robert Stephen Silverman |year=2003 |isbn=9780810847750 |access-date=2020-01-20}}</ref><ref>[https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/jews-in-the-national-football-league-nfl "Jews in Sports: National Football League (NFL)"]</ref><ref name="google">{{cite book|title=The Big Book of Jewish Sports Heroes: An Illustrated Compendium of Sports History and the 150 Greatest Jewish Sports Stars|author=Horvitz, P.S.|date=2007|publisher=Specialist Press International|isbn=9781561719075|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dDyEVDIA3aIC|page=54|access-date=2015-03-10}}</ref> Edelman played [[college football]] at the [[University of Missouri]]. He played 90 games of [[American football]] at [[Guard (American football)|guard]] in the [[National Football League]] for the [[New Orleans Saints]] from 1982 to 1989.<ref>{{cite web|author=Brad Edelman   |url=http://www.nfl.com/player/bradedelman/2513457/profile |title=Brad Edelman, C at |work=Nfl.com |date=2020-01-05 |access-date=2020-01-20}}</ref>

His current occupation is photographer, and he currently resides in New Orleans' [[French Quarter]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bradedelman.com/about/index |title=Brad Edelman Photography |publisher=Bradedelman.com |date=2019-11-13 |access-date=2020-01-20}}</ref> He also does sports analysis for [[WDSU-TV]] in New Orleans.{{citation needed|date=October 2015}}

He was inducted into the St. Louis Jewish Sports Hall of Fame.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://jccstl.com/fitness-recreation/sports-recreation/st-louis-jewish-sports-hall-fame/ |title=St. Louis Jewish Sports Hall of Fame |publisher=St. Louis JCC  |date=1992-07-12 |access-date=2020-01-20}}</ref>

'''John Bradley Dusek''' (December 13, 1950 – June 10, 2024) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[linebacker]] for the [[Washington Redskins]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1974 to 1981. He played [[college football]] for the [[Texas A&M Aggies football|Texas A&M Aggies]].

==Early life==
Dusek was born in [[Longview, Texas]], in 1950.<ref name=ALS>{{cite web|title=ALS Hero: Brad Dusek|author=Katie Kroncke|publisher=ALS Association Texas Chapter|date=January 16, 2020|accessdate=August 4, 2023|url=https://alstexas.org/als-hero-brad-dusek/}}</ref> His father and older brother played [[gridiron football]] for [[Temple High School (Texas)|Temple High School]] in [[Temple, Texas]], and the former for [[Texas A&M University]].<ref name=halloffame>{{Cite web|url=https://wacotrib.com/sports/texas_sports_hall_of_fame/hall-of-fame-profile-dusek-carried-on-temple-family-legacy/article_4c9ff506-83ae-555b-936c-a6b035ff4b25.html|title=Hall of Fame profile: Dusek carried on Temple family legacy|first=John|last=Werner|date=May 1, 2018|work=Waco Tribune-Herald|accessdate=June 12, 2024}}</ref>

==Career==
Dusek attended Temple High School and played for its football team as a [[quarterback]] and [[safety (gridiron football position)|safety]].<ref name=halloffame/> He was selected Parade All-American as a senior.<ref name=TAM/>  He then enrolled at Texas A&M University and played [[Texas A&M Aggies football]] from 1969 to 1972<ref name=PFA>{{cite web|title=Brad Dusek|publisher=Pro Football Archives|accessdate=August 4, 2023|url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/playerd/duse00200.html}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=A&M Dream|newspaper=Corsicana Daily Sun|date=August 9, 1970|page=35|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/corsicana-daily-sun-am-dream/129454445/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Brad Dusek Graduates To Starting Left Halfback|newspaper=Staunton Leader|date=July 31, 1970|page=8|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-daily-news-leader-brad-dusek-graduat/129454275/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> as a [[Fullback (gridiron football)|fullback]] in its [[wishbone offense]]. He was named to the [[1971 All-Southwest Conference football team]]<ref name=obit>{{Cite web|url=https://www.tdtnews.com/news/central_texas_news/article_cbd95b7c-2846-11ef-a09d-7bdf9ac1ac1d.html|title=Temple football legend Dusek dies of ALS|first=Tim|last=Waits|date=June 11, 2024|work=Temple Daily Telegram|accessdate=June 12, 2024}}</ref> and was the Aggies' [[team captain]] in [[1972 Texas A&M Aggies football team|1972]].<ref name=TAM/>

The [[New England Patriots]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL) selected Dusek as [[linebacker]] in the third round and 56th pick of the [[1973 NFL draft]]. They traded him to the [[Washington Redskins]] for [[Donnell Smith]],<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1978/09/04/redskins-butz-dusek-stun-patriots/b3578466-1488-4c39-836a-053755a696f9/|title=Redskins Butz, Dusek Stun Patriots|first=Ken |last=Denlinger|newspaper=Washington Post|date=September 3, 1978|accessdate=June 12, 2024}}</ref> with whom he played 114 games from 1974 to 1981, 97 as a starter. He had 16 fumble recoveries (including three returned for touchdowns), 14 sacks, four interceptions and three touchdowns.<ref name=PFA/> He made over 100 tackles in the 1977, 1978 and 1979 seasons. Michael Richman, in ''The Redskins Encyclopedia'', called him "one of the best outside linebackers in Redskins history".<ref>{{cite book|title=The Redskins Encyclopedia|author=Michael Richmanpublisher=Temple University Press|year=2009|pages=282–283| publisher=Temple University Press |isbn=9781592135448}}</ref>

==Later life==
Dusek had four children.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.tdtnews.com/sports/article_8dd44818-d4ce-11e8-9601-9bd31023e812.html|title=Column: Dusek more than ready, willing to battle ALS|first=Tim|last=Waits|date=October 20, 2018|work=Temple Daily Telegram|accessdate=June 12, 2024}}</ref> After football, he built homes.<ref name=obit/>

Dusek was inducted into the Texas A&M Athletic Hall of Fame in 2014 and the Texas High School Football Hall of Fame in 2018.<ref name=TAM>{{cite web|title=Brad Dusek|publisher=Texas A&M Athletic Hall of Fame|accessdate=August 4, 2023|url=https://12thman.com/honors/texas-am-athletic-hall-of-fame/brad-dusek/2}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Temple's Dusek inducted into Texas High School Football HOF|publisher=KWTC.com|date=May 5, 2018|url=https://www.kwtx.com/content/sports/Temples-Dusek-honored-at-Hall-of-Fame-Induction-481844841.html}}</ref>

Dusek was diagnosed with [[ALS|amyotrophic lateral sclerosis]] (ALS) in September 2018 and declared an "ALS Hero" in 2020 by the Texas Chapter of the ALS Association.<ref name=ALS/> He died on June 10, 2024, at the age of 73.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.kxxv.com/news/local-news/in-your-neighborhood/brad-dusek-a-temple-texas-a-m-nfl-legend-dies-at-73|title=Brad Dusek, a Central Texas football legend, dies at 73|date=June 12, 2024|website=25 News KXXV and KRHD|accessdate=June 12, 2024}}</ref>

'''Bradley Scott Beckman''' (December 31, 1964 – December 18, 1989) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[tight end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[New York Giants]] and the [[Atlanta Falcons]]. He played [[college football]] at the [[University of Nebraska at Omaha]] and was selected in the seventh round of the [[1988 NFL draft]] by the [[Minnesota Vikings]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1988 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1988/draft.htm |access-date=2023-09-23 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

Beckman was killed when the car he was a passenger in bumped a car in front of it and then lost control and was hit broadside by a truck. The accident was on I-85 near Lilburn in icy conditions on December 18, 1989, nearly two weeks before Beckman's 25th birthday. His death was the second one for the Falcons that year, and the third in the space of two years. Four weeks prior, offensive tackle [[Ralph Norwood]] died in a separate traffic collision; a year before, cornerback [[David Croudip]] died of a cocaine overdose.<ref>{{cite web |title=Sports News Briefs; Car Crash Kills Falcon Tight End (Published 1989) |website=[[The New York Times]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220311064301/https://www.nytimes.com/1989/12/19/sports/sports-news-briefs-car-crash-kills-falcon-tight-end.html |archive-date=2022-03-11 |url-status=live |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/12/19/sports/sports-news-briefs-car-crash-kills-falcon-tight-end.html}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1989-12-18-sp-627-story.html |title=Falcons End Brad Beckman Killed |agency=Associated Press |date=December 18, 1989 |website=[[Los Angeles Times]] |access-date=February 11, 2018 |quote=}}</ref> At the time of his death, the Falcons had played 15 out of 16 games in the season. Beckman had played in all 15 games for the Falcons up to that point, starting in two of them.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BeckBr00.htm |title=Brad Beckman Stats |website=pro-football-reference.com |publisher=Pro Football Reference |access-date=February 11, 2018}}</ref>

{{Short description|American football player (born 1978)}} {{good article}} {{Use mdy dates|date=June 2024}} {{Infobox gridiron football person | name = Brad Lekkerkerker | image = | alt = | caption = | birth_date = {{Birth date and age|1978|5|8}} | birth_place = [[Chino, California]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | team = | number = 75 | status = Retired | position1 = [[Offensive tackle]] | height_ft = 6 | height_in = 7 | weight_lb = 330 | high_school = [[Damien High School|Damien]] ([[La Verne, California]]) | college = [[Chaffey Panthers football|Chaffey JC]] (2000–2001)
[[UC Davis Aggies football|UC Davis]] (2002–2003) | undraftedyear = 2004 | pastteams = * [[Houston Texans]] ({{NFL Year|2004}})* * [[Oakland Raiders]] ({{NFL Year|2004|2005}}) | statlabel1 = [[Games played]] | statvalue1 = 1 | career_highlights = }} '''Brad Lekkerkerker''' (born May 8, 1978) is an American former professional football [[offensive tackle]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). From [[Chino, California]], he grew up on his family's dairy farm and did not play [[high school football]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Chaffey Panthers football|Chaffey Panthers]] and [[UC Davis Aggies football|UC Davis Aggies]]. After going unselected in the [[2004 NFL draft]], Lekkerkerker signed with the [[Houston Texans]] as an [[Free agent#Undrafted free agent|undrafted free agent]]. He later was a member of the [[Oakland Raiders]] from 2004 until his retirement in 2006, appearing in one NFL game. His younger brother, [[Cory Lekkerkerker]], also played as an offensive tackle in the NFL. ==Early life== Lekkerkerker was born on May 8, 1978, in [[Chino, California]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/players/l/lekk00200.html|website=Pro Football Archives|title=Brad Lekkerkerker Stats}} His grandparents were immigrants from the Netherlands.{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-sacramento-bee/191040518/|newspaper=[[The Sacramento Bee]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=September 20, 2003|pages=C1, [https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-sacramento-bee/191040633/ C7]|title=Unbreakable Bond|author=Davidson, Joe}} He grew up in Chino and has a younger brother, [[Cory Lekkerkerker|Cory]], who also played in the [[National Football League|NFL]].{{Cite news|url=https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2005/12/02/sundays-feature-sibling-rivalryfirst-nfl-game-with-two-players-named-lekkerkerker/|newspaper=[[The Press Democrat]]|date=December 2, 2005|title=Sunday's Feature: Sibling rivalryfirst NFL game with two players named Lekkerkerker [sic] |author=Barber, Cory}} His father died of cancer when he was age nine. After his father's death, he helped run the family's dairy farm, which included 2,000 cows. Lekkerkerker and his brother both attended [[Damien High School]] in [[La Verne, California|La Verne]], but only Cory played football there, as Brad ran the family farm.{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-sacramento-bee/190884295/|newspaper=[[The Sacramento Bee]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=April 22, 2004|page=32|title=Local players hoping to feel a draft|author=Amick, Sam}}{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/chino-champion/190884761/|newspaper=[[Chino Champion]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=November 22, 2003|page=16|title=Brothers turning heads at UC Davis|author=Thompson, Josh}} In 1996, he graduated from Damien. ==College career== In 2000, following after his brother, Lekkerkerker enrolled at [[Chaffey College]] and began playing football for the first time. ''[[The Sacramento Bee]]'' noted that the first time he ever tried to line up in a [[three-point stance]], he nearly fell down. Nevertheless, as an [[offensive tackle]], he became one of the top-100 ranked [[junior college]] players and was a Junior College [[All-America college football team|All-American]] as a [[sophomore]], while Chaffey won 19 of 22 games in two seasons with the Lekkerkerker brothers. He and his brother started all 22 of those games, one at left tackle and the other at right tackle.{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times/190886031/|newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=April 23, 2004|pages=B1, [https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times/190886222/ B6]|title=Lekkerkerker eyeing the NFL|author=Benson, Jeff}} The brothers received attention from several [[NCAA Division I]] schools, but they both transferred to the [[NCAA Division II]]-level [[UC Davis Aggies football|UC Davis Aggies]] in 2002. Brad had initially received an offer to play for the [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State Buckeyes]], but they retracted their offer upon learning his age and that he would only be eligible for one Division I season due to having attended Chaffey for a semester in 1996. Lekkerkerker and his brother were teammates at UC Davis from 2002 to 2003. As a college [[Junior (education year)|junior]], he stood at {{convert|6|ft|7|in}} and weighed {{convert|310|lb|kg}}, while his brother was {{convert|6|ft|6|in}} and {{convert|300|lb|kg}}, earning the two the nickname the "Brothers Large".{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-sacramento-bee/191040974/|newspaper=[[The Sacramento Bee]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=August 24, 2002|page=34|title=Aggies: Junior college transfers will add bulk}} ''The Bee'' described them as like twins and noted, "They sound alike, in tone and in beliefs. They are quiet and shy by nature, but brutish and unforgiving in shoulder pads." The two brothers started together as offensive tackles for the Aggies in 2003. In total, Lekkerkerker played 22 games at UC Davis, 12 as a starter.{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/chino-champion/191041916/|newspaper=[[Chino Champion]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=May 8, 2004|page=19|title=Lekkerkerker signs with the NFL's Houston Texans|author=Thompson, Josh}} At the conclusion of his collegiate career, he played in the [[East–West Shrine Bowl]].{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-sacramento-bee/191041736/|newspaper=[[The Sacramento Bee]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=December 6, 2003|page=20|title=Five Aggies in all-star games}} ==Professional career== Lekkerkerker was invited to the [[NFL Scouting Combine]] and worked out with the [[Chicago Bears]] and [[New England Patriots]] prior to the [[2004 NFL draft]]; some sources projected him as a potential sixth- or seventh-round pick. He went unselected in the draft and afterwards signed with the [[Houston Texans]] as an [[Free agent#Undrafted free agent|undrafted free agent]]. He was released by the Texans on August 31, 2004, then signed with the [[Oakland Raiders]] [[practice squad]] on September 7, where he remained for the rest of the season. He re-signed with the Raiders on January 4, 2005, but was released on September 3, 2005, after which he re-signed with the practice squad. On November 26, he was promoted to the active roster after [[Warren Sapp]] was placed on [[injured reserve]].{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/san-francisco-chronicle/191043005/|newspaper=[[San Francisco Chronicle]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=November 27, 2005|page=41|title=Sapp is out for season}} He appeared in only one game, a Week 17 loss to the [[New York Giants]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LekkBr20/gamelog/|website=[[Pro Football Reference]]|title=Brad Lekkerkerker Career Game Log|access-date=February 10, 2026}} During the 2005 season, the Raiders twice played against the [[San Diego Chargers]], who had Brad's brother Cory on their roster, although the brothers did not play in the games. After initially re-signing with the Raiders in 2006, Lekkerkerker was placed on the reserve/retired list on July 25, 2006, ending his professional career. After his playing career, Lekkerkerker lived in [[Bakersfield, California]], and became an almond farmer.{{Cite news|url=https://www.dailybulletin.com/2019/09/14/random-thoughts-how-does-horse-racing-rally-after-latest-scandal/|newspaper=[[Daily Bulletin]]|title=Random Thoughts: How does horse racing rally after latest scandal? |date=September 14, 2019|author=Brewster, Louis}} ==References== {{Reflist}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Lekkerkerker, Brad}} [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:1978 births]] [[Category:20th-century American sportsmen]] [[Category:21st-century American sportsmen]] [[Category:American football offensive tackles]] [[Category:Chaffey Panthers football players]] [[Category:UC Davis Aggies football players]] [[Category:Houston Texans players]] [[Category:Oakland Raiders players]] [[Category:People from Chino, California]] [[Category:Players of American football from San Bernardino County, California]] [[Category:American people of Dutch descent]]

'''Brad Leggett''' (born January 16, 1966)  is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Center (American football)|center]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[USC Trojans football|USC Trojans]] and was selected in the eighth round of the [[1990 NFL draft]] by the [[Denver Broncos]]. He played in the NFL for the [[New Orleans Saints]] and [[Detroit Lions]].

==Early life==
Leggett was born in [[Vicksburg, Mississippi]]. His father is former NFL player (12 years) and coach (25 years) [[Earl Leggett]]. He played [[High school football|prep football]] at [[Fountain Valley High School]] in [[Fountain Valley, California]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=LEGGEBRA01 |title=Brad Leggett |publisher=databaseFootball.com |accessdate=November 26, 2012 |url-status=usurped |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20121018073152/http://www.databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=LEGGEBRA01 |archivedate=October 18, 2012 }}</ref> He is in his high school's Hall of Fame after playing football his senior year.

==College career==
Leggett recruited by several colleges and chose to play college football [[college football]] for the [[USC Trojans football|USC Trojans]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nfl.com/player/bradleggett/2501726/profile| title =Brad Leggett | publisher= NFL Enterprises LLC|accessdate= November 26, 2012}}</ref>

During his time at the [[University of Southern California]], Leggett was part of three [[PAC-10]] championship teams, playing in three consecutive [[Rose Bowl Game]]s. Leggett made first-team All-PAC-10 and was chosen to play in the Senior Bowl.  Leggett was honorable mention All-American his senior year at USC.

==Professional career==
Leggett was originally an eighth round selection (219th overall pick) by the [[Denver Broncos]] in the [[1990 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1990 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1990/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-25 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LeggBr20.htm| title= Brad Leggett|publisher= Pro-Football-Reference.com|accessdate= November 26, 2012}}</ref>  He played for the [[New Orleans Saints]] (1990–1991, 1993) and the [[Detroit Lions]] (1992).

Leggett and his father Earl were the first father and son to both play in the Saints franchise history. Leggett’s NFL career was derailed by back injuries forcing him to retire early.

'''Bradley Joseph Cottam''' (born November 28, 1984) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[tight end]] for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL).

==Early life==
Cottam played [[high school football]] at [[Evangelical Christian School]] in [[Cordova, Tennessee]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Evangelical Christian (Cordova, TN) Alumni Pro Stats |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/schools/high_schools.cgi?id=f9dc3e0a |access-date=March 10, 2024 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=ATHLETICS LEGACY |url=https://www.ecseagles.com/athletics/athletics-legacy |access-date=March 10, 2024 |website=Evangelical Christian School |language=en-US}}</ref>

==College career==
Cottam played [[college football]] for the [[Tennessee Volunteers football|Tennessee Volunteers]] under head coach [[Phillip Fulmer]]. He contributed on the field from 2004 to 2007.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Brad Cottam College Stats, School, Draft, Gamelog, Splits |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/brad-cottam-1.html |access-date=March 10, 2024 |website=College Football at Sports-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He caught his first and only collegiate touchdown in his final game. He had a 31-yard reception in the Outback Bowl victory over Wisconsin.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Outback Bowl - Wisconsin vs Tennessee Box Score, January 1, 2008 |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2008-01-01-tennessee.html |access-date=March 10, 2024 |website=College Football at Sports-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

==Professional career==
Cottam was selected by the Chiefs in the third round, 76th overall, of the [[2008 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2008 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2008/draft.htm |access-date=May 12, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=April 28, 2008 |title=Chiefs get depth in draft |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2199&dat=20080428&id=RLoyAAAAIBAJ&sjid=iegFAAAAIBAJ&pg=5747,5895599&hl=en |access-date=February 1, 2016 |work=[[Lawrence Journal-World]]|via=Google News |page=2B}}</ref> After three injury-filled seasons with the Chiefs, he was released on July 29, 2011.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Thorman |first=Joel |date=July 29, 2011 |title=Brad Cottam Released By Kansas City Chiefs |url=https://www.arrowheadpride.com/2011/7/29/2303531/brad-cottam-released-kansas-city-chiefs |access-date=March 10, 2024 |website=Arrowhead Pride |language=en}}</ref>  For his NFL career (2008–09), Cottam caught 16 passes for 183 yard (an 11.4 yards-per-catch average) and no touchdowns.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Brad Cottam Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/C/CottBr00.htm |access-date=March 10, 2024 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

==Personal life==
His younger brother Jeff Cottam also went to Tennessee and was signed by the Cincinnati Bengals as an undrafted free agent in 2010.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jeff Cottam - Football |url=https://utsports.com/sports/football/roster/jeff-cottam/1841 |access-date=March 10, 2024 |website=University of Tennessee Athletics |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Kirkendall |first=Josh |date=April 24, 2010 |title=Bengals Sign S Bryan Evans, Tight End Jeff Cottam, Running Back Cordera Eason |url=https://www.cincyjungle.com/2010/4/24/1442681/bengals-sign-s-bryan-evans-tight |access-date=March 10, 2024 |website=Cincy Jungle |language=en}}</ref>

'''Boyd Efram Jones''' (born May 30, 1961) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player in the [[Tackle (gridiron football position)|offensive tackle]] and [[Guard (gridiron football)|guard]] positions. He played [[college football]] for the [[Texas Southern Tigers football|Texas Southern Tigers]] and later for one season professionally with the [[Green Bay Packers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL).
__TOC__

==Early life==
Jones was born on May 30, 1961, in [[Galveston, Texas]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/J/JoneBo23.htm|website=[[Pro Football Reference]]|access-date=April 24, 2025|title=Boyd Jones Stats}}</ref> After high school, he enrolled at [[Texas Southern University]] (TSU) in 1979, where he played for the [[Texas Southern Tigers football]] team as an [[Tackle (gridiron football position)|offensive tackle]].<ref name="auto3">{{Cite web|url=https://profootballarchives.com/players/j/jone02800.html|website=Pro Football Archives|access-date=April 24, 2025|title=Boyd Jones Stats}}</ref> He attended TSU from 1979 to 1983 and was a four-year starter for the Tigers.<ref name="auto3"/><ref name="auto2">{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/green-bay-press-gazette/171023332/|newspaper=[[Green Bay Press-Gazette]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=August 2, 1984|page=23|title=Free agents: Longshots who long to play|author=McGinn, Bob}} {{Open access}}</ref> Standing at {{convert|6|ft|4|in}} and weighing {{convert|260|lb|kg}}, he and James Grisby were the team's two largest offensive players.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/sun-herald/171023416/|newspaper=[[Biloxi Sun Herald]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=October 17, 1980|page=24|title=SLU wary about Texas Southern}} {{Open access}}</ref> As a [[Junior (education year)|junior]] in 1982, Jones was named second-team All-[[Southwestern Athletic Conference]] (SWAC).<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/clarion-ledger/171023550/|newspaper=[[Clarion-Ledger]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=November 16, 1982|page=24|title=Football}} {{Open access}}</ref>

TSU performed poorly during Jones's tenure with the team, compiling records of 3–8 (1979),<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cfbdatawarehouse.com/data/active/t/texas_southern/1975-1979_yearly_results.php|publisher=[[College Football Data Warehouse]]|via=[[Wayback Machine]]|title=Texas Southern Game by Game Results: 1975-1979|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150906000837/http://www.cfbdatawarehouse.com/data/active/t/texas_southern/1975-1979_yearly_results.php|archive-date=2015-09-06}}</ref> 2–9 (1980), 4–6–1 (1981), 1–9–1 (1982), and 4–6 (1983) in his years there.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cfbdatawarehouse.com/data/active/t/texas_southern/1980-1984_yearly_results.php|publisher=[[College Football Data Warehouse]]|via=[[Wayback Machine]]|title=Texas Southern Game by Game Results: 1980-1984|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150906043242/http://www.cfbdatawarehouse.com/data/active/t/texas_southern/1980-1984_yearly_results.php|archive-date=2015-09-06}}</ref> He played under multiple head coaches at TSU.<ref name="auto2"/> He was scouted by the [[Green Bay Packers]] while in college; one scout recalled that when visiting, the school's offensive line coach was absent, and thus Jones stepped in to the role.<ref name="auto2"/>

==Professional career==
Jones was selected by the [[Houston Gamblers]] in the [[1984 USFL territorial draft]] but did not sign with them.<ref name="auto3"/><ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://profootballarchives.com/transactions/j/jone02800.html|website=Pro Football Archives|access-date=April 24, 2025|title=Boyd Jones Transactions}}</ref> After going unselected in the [[1984 NFL draft]], he signed with the [[Green Bay Packers]] as an [[Free agent#Undrafted free agent|undrafted free agent]].<ref name="auto2"/> Packers offensive line coach [[Jerry Wampfler]] described Jones as inexperienced and called him "green as grass", but Jones soon impressed him as he "was tenacious, had quick feet and was hard to knock off balance", according to the ''[[Green Bay Press-Gazette]]''.<ref name="auto2"/> Considered small for tackle, he was moved to [[Guard (gridiron football)|guard]] during the team's training camp.<ref name="auto2"/> He was described as being a "longshot" to make the team, but nonetheless made the final roster by beating out [[Ron Sams]].<ref name="auto2"/><ref name="auto4">{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-capital-times/171024443/|newspaper=[[The Capital Times]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=August 28, 1984|page=11, [https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-capital-times/171024547/ 13]|title=Ivey survives pressure cooker, earns another shot|author=Punzel, Dennis}} {{Open access}}</ref> Head coach [[Forrest Gregg]] noted that Jones had "really come a long way in a short time. He did a good job at both guard and tackle."<ref name="auto4"/> He made his NFL debut in the team's season-opening win over the [[St. Louis Cardinals (NFL)|St. Louis Cardinals]], and also saw action the following week against the [[Los Angeles Raiders]].<ref name="auto1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/J/JoneBo23/gamelog/|website=[[Pro Football Reference]]|access-date=April 24, 2025|title=Boyd Jones Career Game Log}}</ref> However, he was released by the Packers on September 15, 1984, six days after his second game.<ref name="auto1"/><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/green-bay-press-gazette/93646299/|newspaper=[[Green Bay Press-Gazette]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=September 16, 1984|page=37|title=Dickey remains uncertain|author=Christl, Cliff|author-link=Cliff Christl}} {{Open access}}</ref> He did not sign with another team afterwards, ending his professional career with two games played.<ref name="auto3"/><ref name="auto"/>

'''Bradley Edward Jones''' (born April 1, 1986) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[Green Bay Packers]] in the seventh round of the [[2009 NFL draft]], and played [[college football]] for the [[Colorado Buffaloes football|Colorado Buffaloes]]. With the Packers, he was part of their [[Super Bowl XLV]] team that beat the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]].

==Early life==
Jones played football for [[East Lansing High School]] from 2000-2003. As a senior captain and team MVP, Jones was a First-team All-State selection and All-state Dream Team performer by the [[Detroit Free Press]], when the [[Lansing State Journal]] also named him the Defensive Player of the Year.  During his senior and junior years he earned First-team All-Conference (Capitol Area Athletic Conference), All-area and All-area Dream Team honors by the Lansing State Journal.  The Detroit Free Press made him an All-State special mention honoree his junior year, as he also earned a spot on the First-team All-conference when he was a sophomore.

As a senior, he recorded 117 total tackles (79 solo), 18 tackles for loss, 11 sacks, two fumble recoveries (including one for a 70-yard touchdown), five forced fumbles, four interceptions (with one going for a 30-yard touchdown), 15 quarterback hurries and six pass deflections.  On offense, where he also started at tight end, he reeled in 27 passes and five touchdowns for 501 yards.  As a junior and dual starter once again, he compiled 110 total tackles (62 solo), 11 stuffs for loss, five sacks, four fumble recoveries, two forced fumbles, two interceptions, five quarterback pressures, three pass breakups and one blocked field goal.  He also caught 12 balls and one touchdown totaling 280 yards.  During his sophomore season, he finished with 99 total stops (42 solo), six tackles for loss, two sacks, one recovered fumble, one interception, three quarterback hurries and one pass deflection, while also netting one reception for 30 yards.  [[East Lansing]] was the 9-2 conference champs his senior year, 6-4 his junior season and 13-1 his sophomore year, losing in the second round of the state playoffs.

In addition to football, he lettered four years in [[track & field]], where he competed in the [[200-meter dash]] (21.7 career-best) and the [[110 metres hurdles|110m hurdles]] (14.32 career-best), earning All-area and All-regional runner-up honors as a junior.  He also played basketball as a freshman and sophomore.

==College career==
In 2008 Jones started all 12 games at outside linebacker, earning honorable mention All-Big 12;  He was CU’s co-defensive player of the year, as selected by the coaches (Dave Jones Award).  He racked up 78 tackles, of which 48 were solo and 14 for losses, including seven sacks. He also led the team in quarterback hurries with 14 and also forced two fumbles, had a pass breakup and three chasedowns (near sacks).  In 2007, he started all 13 games including the [[Independence Bowl]] at the “sam” outside linebacker position, and  posted 72 tackles on the year (45 solo), with six for losses including a pair of quarterback sacks.  He also had nine third down stops, seven hurries, five tackles for zero and three passes broken up. In 2006, he played in all 12 games, starting 11 and he finished third on the team in tackles with 72 (41 solo). Though he had a season-low two stops at Kansas, he did make his first career interception against the Jayhawks.  He had six third down stops on the season, and he was credited with half a quarterback sack against Iowa State, the first of his career.  He also had two hurries and a pass broken up. In 2005, he played in all 13 games, including the [[Champs Sports Bowl]] (no starts), making 20 tackles on the year, including 16 solo and one for a loss, to go with two third down stops, a quarterback hurry and pass broken up.  In 2004, he redshirted.

===Green Bay Packers===
Jones was selected by the Packers in the seventh round of the [[2009 NFL draft]], and moved into a starting role during the 2009 season after a season-ending injury to linebacker/defensive end [[Aaron Kampman]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2009 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2009/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-13 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://totalpackers.com/2009/11/a-glimpse-of-the-future-brad-jones-will-start-against-cowboys/ | title=A Glimpse of the Future? Brad Jones Will Start Against Cowboys | date=November 14, 2009 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://archive.jsonline.com/sports/packers/70246497.html?subscriber_login=y | title=Jones creates new dilemma }}</ref> Although taken in a lower round and not said to have many of the qualities expected for an NFL linebacker, Jones surprised many with a high degree of production, accruing four sacks and holding his own for the remainder of the season.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/359438-a-case-for-brad-jones | title=A Case for Brad Jones: Why the Green Bay Packers Don't Need to Draft an OLB | website=[[Bleacher Report]] }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/337256-brad-jones-is-a-forgotten-man-in-merrimankampman-rumors | title=Brad Jones is a Forgotten Man in Merriman/Kampman Rumors | website=[[Bleacher Report]] }}</ref> His work ethic and moral standards were thought very highly of by the Packers' coaching staff.

Jones became the permanent starting outside linebacker when Aaron Kampman signed with the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] during the 2010 offseason. He remained the starter on the right side until he suffered a shoulder injury in a game against the division rival [[Minnesota Vikings]]. He was placed on injured reserve three days later.

On January 1, 2012, during the regular season finale versus the [[2011 Detroit Lions season|Detroit Lions]], Jones tackled a 15-year-old fan who had run onto the field.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/1007094-green-bay-packers-video-watch-brad-jones-tackle-unwelcome-guest-at-lambeau | title=Green Bay Packers Video: Watch Brad Jones Tackle Unwelcome Guest at Lambeau | website=[[Bleacher Report]] }}</ref>

Following the 2011-2012 season, the Packers moved Jones to inside linebacker, where he earned a roster spot as mainly a special teams player. Following season-ending injuries to [[Desmond Bishop]] and [[D. J. Smith (American football)|D.J. Smith]], Jones started every game from week 6 on, including the playoffs, he went on to have his best season as a pro, recording 77 tackles, 2 sacks, 4 passes defensed and one forced fumble. After The 2012-2013, The Packers re-signed Jones to a 3 year $11.25 million dollar contract extension, and released Desmond Bishop, which put Jones and [[A. J. Hawk]] atop the depth-chart for the Packers at middle linebacker for the 2013-2014 season. On February 20, 2015, he was released by the Packers.

===Philadelphia Eagles===
On March 2, 2015, Jones signed a two-year contract with the [[Philadelphia Eagles]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=March 2, 2015 |title=Philadelphia Eagles sign ex-Packers LB Brad Jones |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/philadelphia-eagles-sign-ex-packers-lb-brad-jones-0ap3000000475843 |access-date=March 12, 2015 |website=NFL.com}}</ref> On November 11, 2015, Jones was cut from his contract with the [[Philadelphia Eagles|Eagles]].

'''Bradley James Pyatt''' (born April 16, 1980) is an American entrepreneur and former professional [[American football|football]] player. He played as a [[wide receiver]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) and [[Arena Football League]] (AFL) and was signed by the [[Indianapolis Colts]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 2003. He also played [[college football]] for the [[Kentucky Wildcats football|Kentucky Wildcats]] and [[Northern Colorado Bears|Northern Colorado Bears]]. Pyatt is the founder of the sports nutrition company MusclePharm and co-founder of the plant-based protein bar brand TRUBAR and the cognitive performance supplement brand IQ Pouch.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |date=2019-12-07 |title=Brad Pyatt - Health Advocate and Entrepreneur |url=https://ideamensch.com/brad-pyatt/ |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=IdeaMensch |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Pyatt is an [[Arvada West High School]] graduate and played for long-time high school coaching legend Dave Logan on the Wildcats’ Class 5A 1997 state championship team.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |date=2015-10-06 |title=Former Arvada West football star player Brad Pyatt is back as the team's head coach |url=https://www.yahoo.com/news/former-arvada-west-football-star-194338981.html |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=Yahoo News |language=en-US}}</ref> He was a two-time high school All-American, two-time All-Colorado and All-State selection in 1996 and 1997. He was among the most-sought wide receivers in the country, recruited by over 50 colleges, led by: [[Southern California]], [[Miami]], [[Colorado]], [[Kentucky]], [[Michigan State]], and [[Arizona]].<ref name="DenverChannel">{{cite web|last=Bienvenu|first=Lionel|title=Former Arvada West football star Brad Pyatt returns to lead the team as head coach|url=http://www.thedenverchannel.com/sports/former-arvada-west-football-star-brad-pyatt-returns-to-lead-the-team-as-head-coach|publisher=The Denver Channel.|accessdate=21 November 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160816051029/http://www.thedenverchannel.com/sports/former-arvada-west-football-star-brad-pyatt-returns-to-lead-the-team-as-head-coach|archive-date=16 August 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last=Dyer |first=Etta |title=Ex-NFL star turns to coaching at Arvada West High School |url=https://awestnews.com/features/2023/04/29/ex-nfl-star-turns-to-coaching-at-arvada-west-high-school/ |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=The Westwind}}</ref>

== Football career ==

=== College career ===
Pyatt played at [[University of Kentucky]] and [[University of Northern Colorado]] after graduating high school despite having scholarship offers from Southern California and Miami.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=Brad Pyatt, Arvada West , Wide Receiver |url=https://247sports.com/player/brad-pyatt-74635/ |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=247Sports |language=en-US}}</ref> After 3 years with the [[Kentucky Wildcats]] and multiple injuries, Pyatt transferred to University of Northern Colorado in 2002.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" />

=== Professional career ===

==== National Football League ====
Pyatt was signed by the [[National Football League]]’s (NFL) [[Indianapolis Colts]] as a free agent on July 16, 2003, and then played for three seasons in the [[NFL]] as the Colts' wide receiver.<ref name=":7" /> He returned 19 kickoffs for 544 yards - a 28.6 yard-per-return average - and 12 punts for 110 yards, an average of 9.2 yards per return over his first eight games.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nfl.com/players/bradpyatt/profile?id=PYA622937|title=Brad Pyatt|website=NFL.com}}</ref>

Some of his accomplishments include a 38-yard kickoff return versus the [[Tennessee Titans]] on September 14, 2003, and a 50-yard kickoff return against the [[New Orleans Saints]] on September 28, 2003.  One of the highlights of his playing career is his 90-yard kickoff return versus the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] on October 6, 2003. The Colts recovered from the 21-point deficit at less than four minutes remaining, and won this comeback 38-35 when the play set up a touchdown during overtime. This comeback is considered the third best in NFL to-date by experts and analysts.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |title=Brad Pyatt Stats |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/P/PyatBr00.htm |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

==== Arena Football League ====
Pyatt’s NFL career also included playing for the [[St. Louis Rams]], [[Miami Dolphins]], and [[Pittsburgh Steelers]]. In 2007, he joined the [[Colorado Crush]] as part of the [[Arena Football League]] for 2 years. He retired from playing pro-football in 2008.<ref name=DenverChannel/>

==== Career statistics ====
Pyatt's professional football career spanned from 2003 to 2008 with the [[Indianapolis Colts]] and [[Colorado Crush]]. Over his professional career he caught 165 passes for 1,859 yards and 31 receiving touchdowns, (of which 3 receptions and 14 receiving yards were in the NFL).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.statscrew.com/football/stats/p-pyattbra001|title=Brad Pyatt Statistics on StatsCrew.com|website=www.statscrew.com}}</ref><ref name=":7" />

== Coaching career ==
After his professional football career, Pyatt returned to his alma mater, [[Arvada West High School]] in Colorado, where he served as head football coach in 2014.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pleuss |first=Dennis |date=2024-08-26 |title=Arvada West football dominates Fountain-Fort Carson in Week 0 |url=https://www.coloradocommunitymedia.com/archives/arvada/sports/high-school/article_6949dd49-0976-5fc6-8e08-e8fe27005904.html |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=Colorado Community Media |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":5" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Arvada West Football History |url=https://www.maxpreps.com/co/arvada/arvada-west-wildcats/football/history/ |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=www.maxpreps.com}}</ref> He is the school’s seventh coach in 50 years.<ref name="DenverChannel" /> In 2024, he led the Wildcats to their first playoff win since 2018, defeating Fort Collins 59–29 in the opening round of the Class 5A state tournament.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pleuss |first=Dennis |date=2024-11-11 |title=Arvada West football captures first playoff win since 2018 |url=https://coloradopreps.com/arvada-west-football-captures-first-playoff-win-since-2018/ |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=Colorado Preps |language=en}}</ref>

Pyatt played for legendary Arvada West coach Dave Logan and has revived Logan’s coaching philosophies to train his team with the traditions and legacies of previous teams from the late 1990s.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |date=2018-07-21 |title=Brad Pyatt brings winning tradition back to Arvada West |url=https://www.9news.com/article/sports/high-school/brad-pyatt-brings-winning-tradition-back-to-arvada-west/73-576228979 |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=KUSA.com |language=en-US}}</ref> 

As a coach, Pyatt draws from his experience as a player in the NFL and AFL where he played for Pro Football Hall of Fame coach [[Tony Dungy]], quarterback [[Peyton Manning]], General Manager [[Bill Polian]] of the [[Indianapolis Colts]], and Pro Football Hall of Fame quarterback and [[Colorado Crush]] owner, [[John Elway]]. Pyatt specifically credits Manning and Dungy with teaching him about leadership, preparation, and how to treat people on and off the field.<ref name=DenverChannel/>

During his tenure, he focused on rebuilding the football program and developing student-athletes.<ref name=":8" /> In 2020 he received regional recognition as Coach of the Year.<ref name=":3" />

== Business career ==

=== MusclePharm ===
Pyatt founded MusclePharm, a sports nutrition company, in 2008 and served as its chief executive officer.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Finger |first=Richard |date=January 29, 2013 |title=Billionaire Pharmaceutical Entrepreneur Makes Bet On Fast Growing Supplement Manufacturer: MusclePharm |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/richardfinger/2013/01/29/billionaire-pharmaceutical-entrepreneur-makes-bet-on-fast-growing-supplement-manufacturer-muscle-pharm/#7ec80c4070c9 |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=Forbes}}</ref> Under his leadership, the company entered distribution partnerships with major retailers including GNC.<ref name=":2" />

During Pyatt’s tenure, MusclePharm entered endorsement and promotional relationships with athletes and sports organizations, including golfer [[Tiger Woods]] and collaborations with [[Arnold Schwarzenegger]],<ref>{{Cite web |date=2014-06-18 |title=Woods signs bag endorsement with MusclePharm |url=https://apnews.com/fl-state-wire-co-state-wire-82a51d39b8314e03a839f1d6adb09d90 |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2013-07-30 |title=Arnold Schwarzenegger to Release New Supplement Line |url=https://www.muscleandfitness.com/athletes-celebrities/news/arnold-schwarzenegger-release-new-supplement-line/ |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=Muscle & Fitness |language=en-US}}</ref> and became the official nutrition partner of the [[Ultimate Fighting Championship]] (UFC), [[Major League Baseball]]’s [[Cincinnati Reds]], and European soccer’s [[Manchester City F.C.|Manchester City]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 22, 2011 |title=UFC and MusclePharm Ink New Deal |url=https://www.ufc.com/news/ufc-and-musclepharm-ink-new-deal |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=www.ufc.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Kennedy |first=Mike |date=2015-06-10 |title=MusclePharm signs with City Football Group |url=https://www.sportspro.com/news/musclepharm_signs_with_city_football_group/ |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=SportsPro |language=en-GB}}</ref>

In September 2015, the [[United States Securities and Exchange Commission|U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission]] (SEC) charged MusclePharm and four individuals, including Pyatt, with committing a series of accounting and disclosure violations.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.denverpost.com/2015/09/08/sec-denver-based-musclepharm-hid-perks-and-other-expenses/|title=SEC: Denver-based MusclePharm hid perks and other expenses|date=September 8, 2015}}</ref> The SEC's investigation found that MusclePharm omitted or understated nearly a half-million dollars’ worth of perks bestowed upon its executives, including approximately $244,000 paid to CEO Brad Pyatt related to automobiles, apparel, meals, golf club memberships, and his personal tax and legal services.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sec.gov/news/pressrelease/2015-179.html|title=SEC.gov | SEC Charges Sports Nutrition Company With Failing to Properly Disclose Perks for Executives|website=www.sec.gov}}</ref> MusclePharm and the four individuals settled the cases without admitting or denying the SEC’s findings. MusclePharm agreed to pay a $700,000 penalty and hire an independent monitor for one year among other undertakings. Pyatt agreed to pay a $150,000 penalty.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sec.gov/litigation/admin/2015/33-9904.pdf |title=Brad J. Pyatt |date= |accessdate=2020-04-17}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=SEC Charges Sports Nutrition Company With Failing to Properly Disclose Perks for Executives |url=http://www.sec.gov/news/pressrelease/2015-179.html |website=www.sec.gov |accessdate=17 April 2020 |date=8 September 2015}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

After serving as MusclePharm’s president and CEO for 8 years, Pyatt resigned from the company in March 2016.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.denverpost.com/2016/03/16/musclepharm-founder-brad-pyatt-resigns-as-ceo-after-federal-investigation/ |title=MusclePharm founder Brad Pyatt resigns as CEO after federal investigation |date=March 16, 2016}}</ref> His severance included $1.1 million cash.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2016-10-26/how-musclepharm-went-from-swole-to-twig |title=How MusclePharm Went From Swole to Twig |publisher=Bloomberg |date=2016-10-26 |accessdate=2020-04-17}}</ref>

=== TRUBAR ===
Pyatt later co-founded TRUBAR, a plant-based protein bar brand, with his wife Stephanie Pyatt.<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2020-10-15 |title=Industry Veteran Brad Pyatt and Wife's Vegan Brand Wins 2020 Mindful Award, the Best Vegan Bar of the Year |url=https://apnews.com/press-release/newmediawire/nfl-lifestyle-business-sports-corporate-news-04aebcf56b3b30fb89c612ede542a301 |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=AP News |language=en-US}}</ref> According to reports, TRUBAR was acquired by Turkish company [[Eti (company)|ETİ Gıda]] for C$201 million in 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |date=December 3, 2025 |title=$201M (CAD) Exit for Bar Brand TRUBAR Reported Last Week by CPG Insider – Founded by Former NFL Player Brad Pyatt and His Wife |url=https://finance.yahoo.com/news/201m-cad-exit-bar-brand-005600567.html |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=Yahoo Finance}}</ref>

=== IQ Pouch ===
In 2026, Pyatt launched IQ Pouch, a cognitive performance supplement brand.<ref name=":6" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Ferrer |first=Benjamin |title=IQ Pouch launches nootropic oral pouches for cognitive energy |url=https://www.nutritioninsight.com/news/iq-pouch-paraxanthine-caffeine-energy-focus.html |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=www.nutritioninsight.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=IQ Pouch Launches "Smart Energy" Nootropic Pouches Powered by enfinity® Paraxanthine |url=https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/iq-pouch-launches-smart-energy-nootropic-pouches-powered-by-enfinity-paraxanthine-302706390.html |access-date=2026-03-29 |website= |language=en}}</ref>

'''Brad Nortman''' (born September 12, 1989) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[punter (football)|punter]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Wisconsin Badgers football|Wisconsin Badgers]]. He was selected by the [[Carolina Panthers]] in the sixth round of the [[2012 NFL draft]], making him the first punter that the team had drafted in its history.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Carolina Panthers All-Time Draft History |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/car/draft.htm |access-date=June 9, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en |archive-date=May 26, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180526231747/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/car/draft.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Early life==
Nortman was born and raised in Brookfield, Wisconsin. Nortman attended [[Brookfield Central High School]] in [[Brookfield, Wisconsin]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 18, 2018 |title=Brookfield Central's Brad Nortman in NFL |url=https://www.jsonline.com/picture-gallery/communities/2018/01/18/brookfield-centrals-brad-nortman-in-nfl/109577824/ |access-date=January 31, 2018 |website=Milwaukee Journal Sentinel |language=en |archive-date=April 17, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200417105702/https://www.jsonline.com/picture-gallery/communities/2018/01/18/brookfield-centrals-brad-nortman-in-nfl/109577824/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Nortman was ranked as the No. 4 punter in the nation by [[Rivals.com]] and No. 8 by [[Scout.com]]. He was rated as the fourth-best player in the state of Wisconsin by Scout.com for the 2008 recruiting class.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Brad Nortman, Brookfield Central, Kicker |url=https://247sports.com/Player/Brad-Nortman-5235/high-school-17986/ |access-date=June 9, 2023 |website=247Sports |language=en-US}}</ref> Following his senior season, Nortman was named first-team all-state as a punter, first-team all Greater Metro Conference as a linebacker as well as Greater Metro Conference co-defensive back of the year. He also played tight end garnering honorable mention  Greater Metro Conference honors during his senior year.{{citation needed|date=June 2023}} On February 13th, 2026, Nortman was announced as the first inductee into Brookfield Central's Athletic Hall of Fame for 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |date=March 12, 2026 |title=Brookfield Central Athletic Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony - Class of 2026 |url=https://gofan.co/event/6162443 |access-date=March 12, 2026 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==College career==
Nortman attended the University of Wisconsin from 2008–2011.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Brad Nortman College Stats |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/brad-nortman-1.html |access-date=January 31, 2018 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en |archive-date=February 1, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180201075558/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/brad-nortman-1.html |url-status=live }}</ref> In the 2008 season, he finished with 66 punts for 2,781 net yards for a 41.8 average.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Brad Nortman 2008 Game Log |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/brad-nortman-1/gamelog/2008/ |access-date=January 31, 2018 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en |archive-date=February 1, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180201075545/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/brad-nortman-1/gamelog/2008/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In the 2009 season, he finished with 49 punts for 2,056 net yards for a 42.0 average.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Brad Nortman 2009 Game Log |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/brad-nortman-1/gamelog/2009/ |access-date=January 31, 2018 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en |archive-date=February 1, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180201075458/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/brad-nortman-1/gamelog/2009/ |url-status=live }}</ref> After his sophomore season in 2009, Nortman was named honorable mention All-Big Ten (coaches), [[ESPN the Magazine]] Academic All-District and Academic All-Big Ten. In the 2010 season, he finished with 38 punts for 1,623 net yards for a 42.7 average. Following his junior season in 2010, Nortman was named academic All-Big Ten.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Brad Nortman 2010 Game Log |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/brad-nortman-1/gamelog/2010/ |access-date=January 31, 2018 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en |archive-date=February 1, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180201075229/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/brad-nortman-1/gamelog/2010/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In the 2011 season, he finished with 46 punts for 1,943 net yards for a 42.2 average.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Brad Nortman 2011 Game Log |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/brad-nortman-1/gamelog/2011/ |access-date=January 31, 2018 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en |archive-date=February 1, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180201075319/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/brad-nortman-1/gamelog/2011/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Following the 2011 season, Nortman was named consensus honorable mention All-Big Ten, Academic All-Big Ten and participated in the [[2012 Senior Bowl]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Heller |first=Dave |date=January 28, 2012 |title=Badgers at the Senior Bowl |url=http://www.jsonline.com/blogs/sports/138276649.html |access-date=June 9, 2023 |website=Milwaukee Journal Sentinel |language=en}}</ref> Nortman ranks third in [[Wisconsin Badgers|Wisconsin]] history with a career punting average of 42.1 yards per punt. He is fourth in school history with 8,383 career punting yards and fifth with 199 career punts.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wisconsin Badgers Punting |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/wisconsin/punting.html |access-date=January 31, 2018 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en |archive-date=February 1, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180201075356/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/wisconsin/punting.html |url-status=live }}</ref>
